common_name: Ness' Crinkle Blue African Violet (Ruffled Blue-Flowered Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Ness' Crinkle Blue's ruffled, wavy-edged foliage is part of its ornamental appeal alongside the flowers.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Ness' Crinkle Blue is a named African violet cultivar prized for its distinctive crinkled, ruffled, wavy-edged leaves, a textured foliage trait distinct from the smooth, flat leaves of most African violets, topped with semi-double, deep blue-purple flowers held above the foliage. The keys to success are bright indirect light, bottom-watering or careful top-watering that avoids wetting the crown and leaves, and consistently moist but not waterlogged, slightly acidic potting mix with good aeration. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, and remove spent blooms and any yellowing lower leaves to keep the rosette tidy.

common_name: Rob's Boom Boom African Violet (Bold Red-Purple Bicolor Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Rob's Boom Boom is a named African violet cultivar bred for large, bold, semi-double to double flowers that combine deep wine-red and purple tones in a dramatic, saturated bicolor pattern, standing out strongly against the dark green foliage rosette. The keys to success are bright indirect light, bottom-watering or careful top-watering that avoids wetting the crown and leaves, and consistently moist but not waterlogged, slightly acidic potting mix with good aeration. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, and rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Streptocarpus blooms more continuously than African violet and tolerates slightly cooler temperatures.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, letting the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings. Concord Blue produces trumpet-shaped, rich violet-blue flowers with a fine network of darker throat veining, held in loose clusters on wiry stems well above the long, strap-like, textured leaves that are distinct from the compact rosette of African violet, its close relative. It blooms nearly continuously through the growing season under good light, and tolerates slightly cooler indoor temperatures than African violet, making it a good choice for a bright but unheated sunroom or porch in the cool season. Remove spent flower stems at the base to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every couple of years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Root stolon plantlets or stem cuttings in moist propagating mix; grow as a houseplant or hanging basket in bright indirect light with high humidity. Cleopatra needs consistently warm temperatures above 60°F and struggles in dry indoor air.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with high humidity in a well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist potting mix, in a hanging basket or shallow pot where the trailing stolons can spread. Cleopatra is a heavily variegated flame violet cultivar with quilted, coppery-green leaves splashed irregularly in pink and cream, so striking that the foliage upstages the small, tubular, orange-red flowers that appear intermittently along the spreading, strawberry-like runners. Like other episcias it spreads by producing baby plantlets on the ends of trailing stolons, which root readily when they touch soil, making it easy to propagate and share. It is more particular about warmth and humidity than African violet, declining in cool drafts or dry air, so a terrarium, humidity dome, or consistently warm, humid room suits it best.
